intro: Email list growth rate is the net percentage change in list size over a period, from new subscribers minus unsubscribes. Enter new subscribers, unsubscribes, and the starting list size to get the rate.

sections.heading: How List Growth Rate is calculated
sections.body: List Growth Rate = (New Subscribers − Unsubscribes) ÷ Starting List Size. This calculator's formula is net of unsubscribes only — it does not subtract bounces or spam complaints from the new-subscriber count. Some other definitions of list growth rate do include those as additional losses; check which version a benchmark or report is using before comparing it against this result.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: (500 − 300) ÷ 10,000 = 2.00%. Because the numerator is a net figure, this can also come out negative: 100 new subscribers against 500 unsubscribes on the same 10,000-person list gives (100 − 500) ÷ 10,000 = −4.00%, a genuinely shrinking list, not an error to be blocked.

sections.heading: Not every list growth rate definition counts the same losses
sections.body: [Some published definitions of list growth rate build the loss side of the formula from unsubscribes, bounces, and spam complaints together, not unsubscribes alone](https://count.co/metric/list-growth-rate). This calculator deliberately uses the narrower unsubscribes-only version, matching the two inputs it actually asks for. That's not a mistake in either direction — it's a genuine methodology choice, and it means a rate computed here isn't directly comparable to one computed under a broader bounces-and-complaints-included formula without accounting for the difference.

sections.heading: List Growth Rate vs. Unsubscribe Rate
sections.body: List Growth Rate is a net, list-wide figure over a period — it nets new subscribers against unsubscribes to show whether the list as a whole is expanding or shrinking. [Unsubscribe Rate](/calculators/unsubscribe-rate) is a single-send figure — the share of one campaign's delivered emails that produced an opt-out, with a different denominator (delivered emails for that send, not the list's starting size). A campaign can have a normal, low unsubscribe rate while the list still shrinks overall, if new-subscriber acquisition isn't keeping pace with the unsubscribes accumulating across many sends.

faq.q: What is Email List Growth Rate?
faq.a: List growth rate is the net percentage change in an email list's size over a period, calculated as (new subscribers minus unsubscribes) divided by the starting list size. A positive rate means the list grew; a negative rate means more people left than joined, and the list shrank. This calculator's version nets new subscribers against unsubscribes specifically — some other published definitions of list growth rate also subtract bounces and spam complaints from the new-subscriber total, which is a genuine methodology difference worth checking before comparing rates across sources. Tracking this figure over consecutive periods reveals a growth trend that a single snapshot can't - whether the list is accelerating, plateauing, or steadily shrinking.

faq.q: How do you calculate List Growth Rate?
faq.a: Subtract unsubscribes from new subscribers, then divide by the starting list size: List Growth Rate = (New Subscribers − Unsubscribes) ÷ Starting List Size. A list that starts at 10,000, gains 500 new subscribers, and loses 300 to unsubscribes has a growth rate of (500 − 300) ÷ 10,000 = 2.00%. All three figures need to describe the same time period. Unlike most rate calculators in this set, the result here can legitimately be negative — a list losing more subscribers than it gains is a real, valid outcome, not a data error. Most email platforms track new subscribers and unsubscribes automatically, so pulling this figure typically just means comparing list-size reports across two dates.

faq.q: Can List Growth Rate be negative?
faq.a: Yes, and it's a meaningful result rather than an error. Because the formula nets new subscribers against unsubscribes, a period where unsubscribes outnumber new subscribers produces a negative rate, correctly reflecting a shrinking list. For example, 100 new subscribers against 500 unsubscribes on a 10,000-person list gives (100 − 500) ÷ 10,000 = −4.00%. This calculator doesn't clamp the result at zero, since a negative number is the honest answer when a list is losing people faster than it's gaining them. A shrinking list is worth investigating rather than ignoring, since sustained negative growth eventually reduces the total audience a sender can reach with future campaigns.
